summary: Weekly POC check-in focusing on throughput tuning. Observed higher than expected p95 under bursty traffic; team discussed continuous batching, tuning concurrency caps, and queue shaping. Agreed to run larger synthetic ramp with production prompts and try a short dedicated capacity run.
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-12-29 | Start: 08:23 PST | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Jamie Ortiz (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (NexaBank Eng Lead), Aisha Khan (NexaBank Platform), Tom Liu (NexaBank Product)

[00:00] Jamie Ortiz: Thanks everyone for joining, happy holidays, quick agenda — quick status, dive into the last run numbers, backlog/backpressure behavior, and concrete next steps.
[00:18] Carlos Mendez: yep, thanks. we ran the ramp from Monday night, 6pm to 9pm, used the 2-variant model set: rwd-mini-1 and rwd-oz-lite, mixed traffic 70/30. overall tokens good but p95 spiked.
[00:36] Priya Nair: right, we pulled the traces — looks like continuous batching mostly held, but we saw long tails when concurrency hit 48-50 threads, queue length jumped. queues spilled into our fallback path and we saw model variant cold starts.
[01:00] Aisha Khan: when you say "continuous batching held" — are you talking about automatic prefix batching on the runtime or our manual batch window?
[01:10] Priya Nair: automatic. the runtime does continuous batching at the kernel level, but it defers when concurrency is too high and request shaping kicks in. in this run, the KV cache hit rate fell to ~42%, so more token compute than expected — might be prompt diversity.
[01:33] Tom Liu: we did change the prompt set last week to include longer context for a new flow, that could explain cache. average seq length moved from 120 tokens to 220 tokens.
[01:45] Jamie Ortiz: good callout. so two levers: reduce concurrency targets to keep batch sizes optimal and/or adjust request shaping so that backpressure smooths bursts instead of dropping into fallbacks.
[02:05] Carlos Mendez: latency SLO is 250ms p95 for our user flows, anything above 350ms becomes noticeable. cost is also a constraint — we can't just double hardware.
[02:18] Priya Nair: understood. one idea is conservative concurrency caps during expected peak windows — set a sliding max-concurrency per instance, then let the front-end queue shape. that keeps per-request latency more predictable and preserves batching efficiency.
[02:40] [interruption] Aisha Khan: sorry, quick Q: do we have metrics for queue wait-time distribution?
[02:46] Priya Nair: yes — in the last test the average queue wait was 22ms but p95 queue wait jumped to 420ms at the worst point before fallback. that's what's inflating end-to-end p95.
[03:05] Tom Liu: can we bias batching to favor longer sequences so they commit earlier? that might reduce fragmentation in the batch.
[03:14] Priya Nair: it's possible to do sequence-length aware batching heuristics; we can try priority buckets — long context gets scheduled into dedicated batch slots so it doesn't hold up many small requests. there's a tradeoff because that reduces the statistical batch size for small queries.
[03:34] Jamie Ortiz: also want to call out KV cache warmup. the metric Priya mentioned — 42% hit — we expect ~70% for this workload once prompts are stable. we thought the caching policy was prefix-based, but some tokens are not shared after the prompt change.
[03:52] Carlos Mendez: is that KV cache the same as the "K V cash" you mentioned earlier in the doc? our infra sometimes logs it as kvcache or kvcache-service.
[04:00] Priya Nair: yes, it's kvcache — sorry for slur. the runtime maintains per-session prefix keys and a shared LRU. if prompts diverge, hit rates suffer.
[04:15] [00:04 - 10:00 elapsed]
[04:30] Jamie Ortiz: concrete tuning steps we propose: 1) reduce max concurrency from 60 to 40 on the current host pool; 2) apply request shaping so front-end queues at 150 concurrent requests total across pool; 3) a synthetic run with the 5000-prod prompts.
[04:58] Carlos Mendez: if we reduce concurrency to 40, how much throughput do we lose? the goal is not throughput absolute but stable p95 under 250ms.
[05:10] Priya Nair: we typically see throughput drop ~12-18% when capping concurrency but p95 improves by 35-60% depending on KV hit rates. with a dedicated trial we can tune the kernel selection to win back some throughput via quantization profiles.
[05:30] Tom Liu: can you explain kernel selection? I saw a line in your docs that says "compilation and kernel selection" — is that an offline compile step?
[05:40] Priya Nair: yes, the runtime chooses optimized kernels per model and sequence length. we have thinner kernels for quantized int8 that reduce latency per token. for long sequences sometimes a different attention kernel is faster. we can precompile per-candidate config for your bench.
[05:58] Aisha Khan: what about fallbacks? earlier you said requests spilled to fallback variant and we saw cold start. describe that path.
[06:08] Priya Nair: fallback policy is: if request queue exceeds configured depth, route to a cheaper model variant or region. but that creates model switch cost — extra latency and cold cache. for your workload we recommend increasing queue depth slightly and using a soft-degrade (throttled tokens) instead of immediate model switch.
[06:30] Carlos Mendez: ok. I'd rather increase queue depth if that avoids falling to cheaper models. the user impact of slightly longer wait is better than degraded answers.
[06:40] Jamie Ortiz: noted. also we need to validate memory pressure — when queueing increases we sometimes see increased GPU memory footprint from concurrent KV cache lookups which triggers evictions. we'll instrument memory metrics for next run.
[06:58] [00:06 - 20:00 elapsed]
[07:12] Priya Nair: on instrumentation: we'll enable per-request trace IDs in the next run and provide the CSV with columns: timestamp, model_variant, seq_length, queue_wait_ms, batch_size_at_send, kv_hit. that will let you correlate spikes.
[07:30] Carlos Mendez: perfect. we will add session IDs on our side. also want to validate tokenization differences — sometimes tokenizer mismatch causes longer token counts and weird cache misses.
[07:44] Jamie Ortiz: good point — please send a few raw prompt examples; we'll token-compare with our tokenizer. Tom, can you share product scenarios that are most latency sensitive?
[07:56] Tom Liu: two flows: interactive chat where users expect sub-300ms p95, and background batch generation where p99 is tolerable. interactive is higher priority.
[08:08] Priya Nair: then we should place interactive on a dedicated pool with low-noise SLOs and slightly stricter concurrency. background can be routed to a mixed pool with burst smoothing.
[08:20] Aisha Khan: would that be Redwood Dedicated or can it be done in hosted with routing rules?
[08:27] Jamie Ortiz: both. hosted with strict routing and reserved tokens can emulate dedicated behavior for short trials, but Dedicated gives pinned GPU capacity and predictable latency. Dedicated is part of the enterprise contract if you want month-long reserved runs.
[08:42] Carlos Mendez: budget: can we do a 48-hour dedicated trial for evaluation before committing?
[08:48] Jamie Ortiz: yes, we can do a short reserved pool trial; I'll send terms. that's one of the next steps.
[08:55] [00:09 - 30:00 elapsed]
[09:02] Priya Nair: proposed experiment matrix for the next run: A) concurrency cap 40, default batching; B) concurrency cap 40 + sequence-aware batching; C) trial on dedicated 2x GPU with same traffic; each run 2 hours during peak window. we'll capture 95/99, kv hit, and cost/time.
[09:24] Carlos Mendez: sounds good. how do we measure regression on quality? some quantization profiles can change output; we need to ensure answer quality is stable.
[09:36] Priya Nair: we'll run the same eval prompts and compute similarity/ROUGE-ish scores plus a human spot check for the top 100 outputs. Redwood Optimize can surface regression alerts.
[09:50] Tom Liu: will the runtime do automatic model fallback on quality regressions?
[09:56] Priya Nair: not automatic; regression alerts trigger a configured policy — either block deploy or route to previous variant. we don't auto-switch models without a policy defined.
[10:08] Carlos Mendez: good. also, security question — if we run dedicated on your infra vs private deployment, data residency and KMS requirements differ. we need SOC2 plus customer-managed keys.
[10:20] Jamie Ortiz: we can do Dedicated with BYOK (bring your own keys) via KMS integration; for full customer-managed plane we'd look at Redwood Private which is a bit heavier but meets strict residency. I'll include the security matrix in the follow-up.
[10:33] Aisha Khan: send the SOC 2 report and the audit logs retention details. we need at least 13 months of logs.
[10:40] Jamie Ortiz: noted.
[10:45] [00:10 - 40:00 elapsed]
[10:57] Priya Nair: quick note on queue shaping: front-end token bucket smoothing with a low-pass filter can drastically reduce burst pressure. it adds a few ms to average latency but reduces p95 by smoothing peaks.
[11:12] Carlos Mendez: ok that's acceptable. our SLA is p95 interactive under 250ms, allowing average to move by 10-15ms is fine.
[11:22] Tom Liu: what's the expected improvement if kv hit goes to 70%?
[11:27] Priya Nair: ballpark: going from 42% to 70% hit could cut token compute by ~22-30% and reduce p95 by similar margin in high-contention cases. will depend on sequence length but it's a big lever.
[11:44] Jamie Ortiz: summary and proposed timeline: Carlos uploads prompt corpus by 12/31; Redwood runs synthetic 2-hour runs between 12/31 and 01/02 with variations A/B/C; one dedicated 48-hour trial tentatively Jan 4-6; Redwood sends benchmark sheet and security materials by 01/01.
[12:05] Carlos Mendez: sounds good. minor ask — can we get the run logs in a format we can ingest into our internal observability? JSON lines preferable.
[12:12] Priya Nair: yes, we'll provide ndjson with traceID mapping.
[12:18] Tom Liu: also, please add a column for batch composition at dispatch, that's helpful.
[12:22] Priya Nair: will do.
[12:28] Jamie Ortiz: ok last bits: I'll throw these notes into the CRM and send calendar invites for the dedicated trial. Priya will own the run config. Carlos will own providing prompts. Aisha will validate security artifacts.
[12:40] Carlos Mendez: thanks — appreciate the clear plan.
[12:44] Jamie Ortiz: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and links. Happy holidays and we'll reconvene after the runs.

References shared during call:
- Benchmark sheet: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/nexa-sample (shared)
- Security matrix and SOC2: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 (sent via CRM)

End of transcript.
